title: Test day six
hookLine: notice what's missing: why does Genesis say God finished on the seventh day, the day of rest?
tomorrow: how many times should you think something over?

lines: A LIST OF EVERYTHING YOU DID.
IT'S ALL MADE BY DAY SIX.
cards: A to-do app will happily show you every box you checked today. It has no box for what isn't on the list. Here's an odd line near the start of the Bible.

God makes the world, day by day, and by the end of the sixth day it's all there. Then Genesis says, in the King James Version: "And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made." On the seventh day?
Nothing was made on the seventh day. So what was still missing?

teach.h: WHAT DID THE WORLD LACK? REST.
teach.b: The rabbis noticed it too. In Genesis Rabbah, an early collection of their readings, and later in Rashi, the medieval commentator, the answer comes as a riddle. What did the world lack?
Rest. When the Sabbath came, rest came, and then the work was finished. So rest isn't the empty space after creation.
In this reading it's the last thing created.

The next verse goes further: "And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it." Abraham Joshua Heschel, a modern rabbi, pointed out that the first thing the Bible calls holy is not a mountain or an altar but a day.
That's the teaching behind Shabbat. Shabbat runs from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall, kept with candles, blessings, a long meal, and a rest from work. Not a break from the week.

The week's finish. Something to pass on tonight: by this reading, a world with everything in it was still unfinished, because nothing in it was resting. So on day six of a test, look for what's missing.
Some gaps are flaws. Some are the very thing that would finish it. If your rule is all doing, the rabbis' riddle asks a fair question: where's the seventh day?

how: Shabbat runs from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall, with candles, blessings, meals and a rest from work. On a personal rule, the test week's sixth day is a time to note what the rule leaves out, including rest.

s: Genesis says God ended his work on the seventh day
"and on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made."
in the rabbis' reading, rest is just the gap after the real work
they read rest as the last thing created: when it came, the work was finished.
a day of rest is only about being tired
God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it: set apart, not just recovery.

games.q: your team ships a big project on Friday. your manager says it isn't finished until everyone takes Monday off. by the rabbis' reading of Genesis 2:2, is she right?
o: no: the work ended when the last task was done.
yes: rest is the last piece; without it the work isn't finished.
only if the project ran late and people are worn out.
games.why: the rabbis asked what the world still lacked on the seventh day. rest. when it came, the work was finished.

practice: For this sit, do nothing that counts as doing: hands open, no planning, no fixing. Call it a seventh-day minute. Near the end, let one question rise on its own: what is my rule missing?

wordCard.voice: Test day six: the day you notice what your rule is missing. In the rabbis' riddle, the world was missing rest.

orig.note: Hebrew: rest, the thing the world lacked in the rabbis' riddle on Genesis 2:2.

carryVoice: Keep this one: missing, and sometimes the gap is what finishes the work. See you tomorrow.
